Filed by Claude (head, session 7, claudex opus) from CI triage of PR #884.

## What fails

`server/maintenance/maintenance.pg.test.ts:353` — "maintenance runtime lease boundary (live Postgres) > dead-letters an expired lease that has consumed its attempts instead of reclaiming it": `expect(recovered.state).toBe("succeeded")` got `"running"`.

Observed on CI run 33039270900 (job 98408937958) for #884, whose diff does not touch `server/maintenance/`. The four sibling lease-boundary tests in the same file passed in the same run, and the anti-skip guard emitted nothing, so this is neither a database outage nor a manifest defect.

## Why

`maintenance.pg.test.ts:335` does `await runtime.runner.runOnce();` and reads the reclaimed row at `:352` immediately. `runOnce()` resolved after the claim but before the reclaimed row's handler finished, so the row was still `running`.

## Open question (decides where the fix goes)

Is `runOnce()` contractually required to await every handler it started? If yes, this is a runner defect in `server/maintenance/` and the test is right. If no, the test should wait for the reclaimed row to leave `running` before asserting. The triage lane did not read the runner source; whoever takes this reads `server/maintenance/` first and states which side owns it.

## Done means

- The owning side is named in a comment with the file:line of the contract.
- The fix lands with a done-means script under `scripts/done-means/` that runs the test 20 times against `bun run test:isolated` and exits 1 on any failure (RED to be shown on the pre-fix sha if reproducible locally).

### Direction taken and why — PR #899 body

> ## Summary
>
> - Closes #889. The maintenance lease-boundary expiry test drove the composed runtime with `await runtime.runner.runOnce()` and then read the reclaimed row back immediately. `runOnce()` awaits `tick()` only (`src/maintenance-queue.ts:744`), and `tick()` dispatches each claimed job into the runner's `active` set WITHOUT awaiting it (`:826-831`) so `concurrency` means anything at all; the only method contracted to await handlers is `stop()` (`:754-762`). The read therefore raced the handler, and it is a race the test usually wins — which is why `expect(recovered.state).toBe("succeeded")` reached CI three times on branches that never touched the file.
> - `readSettledRow()` polls the durable row until it leaves `running`/`queued` rather than sampling once. Its deadline keeps a genuinely stuck job from hanging the suite and names the job's last observed state when it fires, so a real regression reports what the row was doing instead of a bare timeout.
> - Refs #878. The pre-commit gate refused this commit on `node/no-process-env` and `max-lines-per-function`, and no exemption was taken, so the file's standards debt is paid here and the change doubles as this file's #878 conversion. The suite now calls `requireTestDatabaseUrl()` at module scope instead of reading the environment and downgrading itself to `describe.skip` — a self-skip reports `0 pass, N skip, 0 fail` and exits 0, which at the exit code is indistinguishable from a suite that ran.
> - The single 268-line describe is split into four grouped by subject — shutdown drain, lease expiry, failure classification, composition — each well under 100 code lines, over shared module-scope helpers (`runtimeFor`, `recordingHandler`, `clearOwnJobs`) rather than duplicated setup. The file stays one module at 339 code lines, so no sibling file was needed.
> - Every suite name keeps the literal `(live Postgres)` marker, since `scripts/assert-db-tests-ran.ts` matches suites by name. That guard registers the four new names with their observed counts (2, 1, 1, 2) in place of the one entry of 5, so an entire subject silently ceasing to run is caught rather than absorbed by the others' count. `MIN_TOTAL_LIVE_TESTCASES` moves 74 → 75 by the net change.

> - Highest-risk behavior: the poll deadline in `readSettledRow()`. At 5s it is generous for a handler that only pushes an id, but a loaded CI machine is the environment where both the original race and this wait matter most. A deadline that fires reports the row's last observed state by name, so the failure would be diagnosable rather than a bare timeout — but it would still be a failure, and the honest position is that 20 local iterations do not prove CI's timing.

### rodaddy — 2026-08-27T06:22:44Z

## Ownership verdict: the TEST owns it, not the runner

Read `src/maintenance-queue.ts` (the runner `MaintenanceQueueRunner` that `server/maintenance/index.ts` composes).

`runOnce()` is `src/maintenance-queue.ts:744-753` — it awaits `this.tick()` and nothing else.

`tick()` ends at `src/maintenance-queue.ts:826-831`:

```ts
for (const job of jobs.slice(0, available)) {
  let active: Promise<void>;
  active = this.execute(job).finally(() => this.active.delete(active));
  this.active.add(active);
}
```

The dispatch is deliberately NOT awaited — the handler promise is put into `this.active` and the loop moves on. That is the design, not an oversight: the runner is concurrent (`available = this.concurrency - this.active.size`, `src/maintenance-queue.ts:772`), and awaiting each handler inside the tick would serialize the whole thing and defeat `concurrency`.

The drain point is `stop()`, `src/maintenance-queue.ts:754-762`, which is the only method contracted to await handlers:

```ts
await this.tickPromise;
while (this.active.size > 0) {
  await Promise.all([...this.active]);
}
```

So `runOnce()` legitimately resolves after the claim and dispatch, before handlers settle. The sibling invariant-1 test in the same file already depends on exactly this (`server/maintenance/maintenance.pg.test.ts` "drains a job whose claim was already in flight when stop() began" — its whole premise is that dispatch and completion are separated).

Per the issue's own open question, that puts the fix on the test side: `server/maintenance/maintenance.pg.test.ts:352` must wait for the reclaimed row to leave `running` before asserting, with a deadline that fails under a named error rather than reading once.

Making `runOnce()` await handlers would be a behavior change to production concurrency semantics to satisfy a test — the larger change, and the wrong boundary.
